question: Why do you want to study Illustration?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific pull toward illustration as a discipline, not just a general love of drawing.

bullets: Name a concrete moment or body of work that pulled you toward illustration specifically
Distinguish illustration from fine art or graphic design in your own words
Show ongoing practice, not just an interest you've had once
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've always drawn, but it became illustration for me when I started making zines in year eleven and realised I loved solving a brief as much as I loved the drawing itself. I like that illustration has to communicate something to someone else, it's not just self-expression, there's a problem to solve. I've kept a weekly sketchbook practice going for almost two years now because I genuinely can't stop making images that tell small stories.

commonMistakes: Saying only 'I've always loved drawing' with nothing more specific
Not distinguishing illustration from fine art
No evidence of sustained practice
followUps: What's the difference between illustration and fine art, to you?

question: Why do you want to study Illustration at this institution specifically?
lookingFor: Specific, researched reasons tied to the course structure, staff, or facilities, not generic praise.

bullets: Reference something concrete about the course, such as a module, studio, or visiting tutor
Connect it to your own practice or gaps you want to fill
Show you've looked at graduate work or the course's specialisms
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked through last year's degree show online and noticed how much of the third-year work moves into publishing and self-authored books, which is exactly the direction I want to push toward. Your course also runs a live brief with a children's publisher in second year, and since I've never had real client feedback, that felt like the missing piece in my practice. I want to be somewhere that treats illustration as a professional discipline, not just a drawing course.

commonMistakes: Generic praise that could apply to any art school
Citing only rankings or reputation
No evidence of having looked at actual course content or student work
followUps: What would you want to get out of that live brief specifically?

question: What first drew you to drawing and making images?
lookingFor: An honest, specific memory that shows early and sustained visual curiosity.

bullets: Give a real, specific memory rather than a vague claim
Show how that early spark developed rather than staying static
Connect it lightly to who you are as a maker now
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My grandmother used to get the newspaper's Sunday comic strip and I'd copy the characters out before I could really read. That turned into filling notebooks with my own strips through primary school, and by secondary school I was doing commissions for classmates' D&D characters for pocket money. It's stayed the same thread the whole way through, just with better technique now.

commonMistakes: A vague 'I've always liked art' with no memory attached
Describing only recent interest with no history
Sounding rehearsed rather than genuine
followUps: How has your drawing changed since then?

question: Talk me through a piece in your portfolio you're proudest of.
lookingFor: Ability to discuss process, decisions, and outcome clearly, not just describe the finished image.

bullets: State the brief or intention behind the piece
Explain a key decision, such as a composition or material choice, and why you made it
Reflect honestly on what worked and what you'd change
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: There's a spread I made for a self-set brief reimagining a local folk tale about a fox that steals the tide. I chose to work in cut paper and gouache because the story felt tactile and layered, like something you could physically peel back. The composition took three attempts because my first version put the fox too centrally and lost the sense of the tide sweeping in, so I pushed it to the edge of the frame instead. I still think the color balance in the sky is a bit flat, and if I redid it I'd push more contrast into that top third.

commonMistakes: Only describing subject matter, not decisions
No honest reflection on weaknesses
Can't explain why a choice was made when pressed
followUps: What would you change if you revisited it now?

question: Which illustrator's work do you keep coming back to, and why?
lookingFor: A specific, well-understood influence with clear reasons, not a name-drop.

bullets: Name a specific illustrator, not just a general style or era
Explain concretely what you study in their work, such as mark-making, color, or pacing
Show how it's affected your own work, not just admiration
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I keep returning to Shaun Tan, especially The Arrival. What gets me is how he builds an entire wordless narrative through incredibly dense, textured drawing, so you have to slow right down to read it. I've started trying to leave more visual information in the margins of my own spreads instead of centering everything, which is directly lifted from watching how he distributes attention across a page.

commonMistakes: Naming an illustrator with no specifics about their work
Choosing someone purely for name recognition
No connection made to their own practice
followUps: Is there anything in their approach you'd push back on?

question: How would you explain the difference between illustration and fine art?
lookingFor: A clear, non-dismissive understanding of both fields and where illustration sits.

bullets: Center the idea of communication or a brief as core to illustration
Avoid implying fine art has no purpose or illustration has no personal voice
Acknowledge the overlap and blurred edges rather than a rigid line
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: For me illustration usually starts with a communication task, a story to tell, a product to sell, a concept to explain to someone else, whereas fine art can be entirely self-directed. But I don't think that makes illustration less personal, my voice still comes through in how I solve the brief. And plenty of work sits right on the line, editorial cartoonists especially, so I try not to treat it as a strict divide.

commonMistakes: Claiming illustration has no personal expression
Dismissing fine art as pointless or self-indulgent
Giving a definition with no examples
followUps: Can you think of an artist who blurs that line?

question: What is editorial illustration, and what makes a good one work?
lookingFor: Understanding of the genre's function and constraints, ideally with a real example.

bullets: Explain that editorial illustration accompanies articles or op-eds, translating an argument into an image
Note the tight turnaround and abstract-thinking demands of the genre
Reference a real example or publication
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Editorial illustration runs alongside news articles or opinion pieces, usually turning around in a day or two, and the job is to capture the argument of the piece in a single striking image rather than illustrate it literally. I love the New York Times op-ed illustrations for that reason, the best ones find a visual metaphor, like showing a policy debate as two people pulling a rope that's actually a road. It's a completely different skill from narrative illustration because you're compressing an idea, not extending a story.

commonMistakes: Confusing editorial illustration with book illustration
No mention of the fast turnaround or conceptual demand
No concrete example
followUps: Can you think of a strong editorial illustration you've seen recently?

question: How do you go about designing a character from scratch?
lookingFor: A concrete, ordered process showing thought about personality, not just appearance.

bullets: Start from personality, role, or story rather than only visual style
Describe iterating on silhouette, proportion, or shape language
Mention testing the character in different poses or expressions
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I start with a paragraph about who the character actually is, their age, what they want, what they're afraid of, before I draw a single line, because that shapes every visual decision after. Then I do quick silhouette thumbnails, ten or so, just black shapes, to find a body language that reads instantly. Once I've picked a direction I test the character in a few different expressions and a walking pose to check the design still holds up when it moves, not just in one perfect stance.

commonMistakes: Jumping straight to rendering without thinking about personality
Only ever drawing one pose or expression
No iteration, first idea treated as final
followUps: How do you know when a character design is finished?

question: Do you prefer working digitally or traditionally, and why?
lookingFor: An honest preference backed by reasoning about the work, with openness to the other medium.

bullets: State a genuine preference with a concrete reason tied to your work
Show awareness of what the other medium offers
Avoid dismissing either medium as inferior
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I default to traditional media, mostly gouache and ink, because I like that mistakes are permanent and force me to commit to decisions rather than endlessly undo them. But I've started scanning my paintings and doing color correction and compositing digitally, which lets me combine the texture of paint with more flexibility in layout. I don't think either is more legitimate, digital painting takes just as much skill, it's just not where my hand feels most natural yet.

commonMistakes: Claiming one medium is objectively better
No reasoning behind the preference
Showing no experience with the medium not chosen
followUps: What would push you to work more digitally?

question: Do you keep a sketchbook, and how do you use it?
lookingFor: Evidence of a genuine, regular observational or idea-generating habit, not a performance for the interview.

bullets: Describe a real, specific habit rather than a vague claim
Distinguish between observational drawing and idea development if relevant
Show what the sketchbook has actually fed into
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I carry a small sketchbook everywhere and try to draw one thing from observation every day, usually people on the bus or objects on my desk, just to keep my hand loose. I keep a separate, messier book for idea development, thumbnails, color notes, bits of writing, that's much less precious and half the pages are crossed out. A few of my strongest final pieces started as a two-second thumbnail in that second book that I almost threw away.

commonMistakes: Claiming to sketch daily with no specifics when pressed
Describing a sketchbook as only for finished-looking work
No connection between sketchbook and final pieces
followUps: Can you describe a specific page that led somewhere unexpected?

question: Tell us about a time your work received harsh feedback. How did you respond?
lookingFor: Genuine openness to critique with a specific example of using it productively, not defensiveness.

bullets: Describe a real piece of criticism rather than a softened version
Show you separated the feedback from your ego and evaluated it fairly
Explain a concrete change that came from it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A tutor once told me a book cover I was proud of read as cluttered and that the typography I'd hand-lettered was fighting the image rather than supporting it. My first reaction was defensive, I'd spent hours on that lettering, but sitting with it for a day I realized she was right, I'd prioritized a technique I liked over what the piece actually needed. I redid the cover with much simpler set type and the composition immediately breathed better. Now I try to ask myself in every piece whether a choice is serving the work or just serving my ego.

commonMistakes: Choosing an example that isn't real criticism
Getting defensive or dismissing the feedback in the retelling
No concrete change resulting from it
followUps: How do you tell good critique from feedback you should ignore?

question: What do you think about when composing an image?
lookingFor: Basic working knowledge of compositional principles applied with intention, not just terminology.

bullets: Mention at least one concrete principle such as focal point, eye path, or balance
Explain why it matters for reading an image, not just as a rule
Show it's something you actively test, such as through thumbnails
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The first thing I think about is where I want the eye to land first and where it should travel next, so I usually block in a value thumbnail before any detail to check the read works in black and white. I try to avoid splitting the image evenly down the middle because it tends to stall the eye, so I'll push the focal point off-center and use smaller shapes to lead toward it. It's less about following rules like the rule of thirds exactly and more about testing whether the image actually guides someone's attention the way I intend.

commonMistakes: Naming rules like the rule of thirds with no explanation of why they matter
No mention of testing composition through thumbnails or sketches
Treating composition as purely decorative
followUps: Can you think of an image where the composition breaks a rule effectively?

question: How do you use color to support the mood of a piece?
lookingFor: Practical, working understanding of color relationships rather than textbook recitation.

bullets: Reference a concrete relationship, such as complementary contrast or a limited palette
Connect color choice to mood or narrative intent, not decoration
Give a real example from your own work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I usually start by picking a limited palette before I even sketch, because too many colors early on tends to muddy the mood I'm going for. For a piece about a stormy harbor I stuck to mostly cool blues and grays and let one warm orange lighthouse glow act as the only high-contrast note, which pulled the eye there and made the whole scene feel colder by comparison. I think about color temperature more than hue names now, since warm against cool usually does more emotional work than picking pretty colors.

commonMistakes: Reciting color wheel terminology with no applied example
Choosing colors decoratively with no link to mood
Using too many colors with no clear hierarchy
followUps: Have you ever deliberately used a jarring color palette? Why?

question: How do you tell a story in a single, still image?
lookingFor: Understanding of narrative compression, implied time, and visual clues.

bullets: Discuss choosing a moment that implies what came before and after
Mention using details or clues that reward a second look
Show awareness of body language and framing as narrative tools
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I try to avoid picking the most obvious moment of an action, like the punch itself, and instead choose the moment just before or after, because that forces the viewer to fill in the story themselves. Small details do a lot of work too, a dropped object, a shadow that doesn't match the figure, something that rewards someone who looks twice. Body language matters most though, the tilt of a shoulder or where someone's eyes are looking can imply an entire relationship without a single word.

commonMistakes: Choosing the most literal, obvious moment with nothing implied
Overloading the image with text or captions instead of visual storytelling
No mention of body language or framing
followUps: Can you give an example of a detail you used to reward a closer look?

question: What's different about illustrating for children compared to illustrating for adults?
lookingFor: Understanding of the specific craft demands of children's illustration, not condescension toward the genre.

bullets: Mention the pairing of image and text across a page turn as a structural challenge
Note the need for clarity of expression and readable emotion for young readers
Push back on the idea that it's simpler or lesser than illustration for adults
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Picture books are as much about pacing across page turns as they are about any single image, you're designing the rhythm of a reveal, what's hidden until the next spread. Characters also need very readable emotion, since young readers are reading the pictures as closely as the words, sometimes more closely. I actually think it's a harder discipline than people assume, because you have far less room to hide behind rendering, the storytelling has to carry everything.

commonMistakes: Treating children's illustration as easier or less serious
No mention of page-turn pacing or spread structure
Focusing only on cute character design
followUps: Have you tried structuring a story across a page turn yourself?

question: Where do you draw the line between using reference images and copying someone else's work?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning about reference use, attribution, and originality, not a rigid or naive answer.

bullets: Distinguish using reference for structure or lighting from tracing or copying composition wholesale
Acknowledge the difficulty of the line and reason through it rather than giving a snap rule
Mention practical habits like using multiple references or your own photography
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I use reference constantly, for anatomy, lighting, folds in fabric, but I try to never build a whole composition from a single source, I'll pull from several photos or take my own reference so nothing traces one specific image. If I'm using someone else's photograph directly for a pose I ask myself whether the final piece could be mistaken for a copy of their framing and choices, not just the same subject. It's genuinely a blurry line in places, especially with photo-realistic styles, so when I'm unsure I lean toward changing more and asking a tutor.

commonMistakes: Claiming reference is never a concern
Giving an overly rigid rule with no nuance
No practical strategy for avoiding the problem
followUps: What would you do if you realized after finishing a piece that it looked too close to a photo you'd used?

question: What's your view on AI image generation and what it means for illustrators?
lookingFor: A thoughtful, non-reactive position that shows the applicant has actually thought about the issue.

bullets: Acknowledge both the genuine threat to livelihoods and any legitimate uses
Avoid a purely dismissive or purely uncritical stance
Connect it to what illustrators can offer that generation tools can't, such as intent and authorship
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I take it seriously rather than dismissing it, it's already affecting commission work and the training data question is a real harm to living artists who never consented. At the same time I don't think it removes the value of a human illustrator, because what I'm actually selling is a specific point of view and the ability to solve a client's problem through conversation, not just an image. I'd rather engage with the debate honestly, including supporting things like opt-out registries and clearer labeling, than either panic or pretend it isn't happening.

commonMistakes: Dismissing the issue as irrelevant to their future career
A purely emotional rant with no reasoned position
Showing no awareness of the training-data consent debate
followUps: Would you ever use AI tools in your own process? Under what conditions?

question: How do you think about developing your own style versus being versatile enough to take on different briefs?
lookingFor: Understanding that style emerges from consistent decisions and habits, and awareness of the commercial value of range.

bullets: Explain style as an emergent set of recurring decisions rather than something chased directly
Acknowledge that professional illustration often demands adapting to a brief
Give an example of a consistent habit or choice that shows up across your work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think you can force a style by copying a look, it tends to come out of the choices you keep making without noticing, for me that's flattened perspective and a fairly limited, muted palette that shows up whether I mean it to or not. But I also know most working illustrators have to flex for a brief, a children's publisher wants something different from a tech magazine, so I've been deliberately practicing tighter, cleaner linework alongside my looser painted work. I'd rather be known for a strong point of view that can bend than a rigid formula that can't.

commonMistakes: Claiming to have a fully formed 'signature style' with no development shown
Treating versatility as having no identity at all
No concrete example of a recurring habit or choice
followUps: What's a stylistic habit you keep noticing in your own work?

question: A client asks for major changes to a piece two days before the deadline. What would you do?
lookingFor: Practical, professional problem-solving that balances client needs with realistic craft constraints.

bullets: Clarify what's actually being asked before reacting, rather than assuming the worst
Weigh what's feasible in the time available and communicate honestly about trade-offs
Show willingness to negotiate scope or timeline rather than either refusing or overpromising
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: First I'd want to understand exactly what's changed and why, sometimes a big-sounding request is actually a small technical fix, and it's worth a quick call rather than assuming. If it genuinely is a major change, I'd be honest about what's realistic in two days and offer options, maybe a simplified version of the change now with a fuller revision after the deadline if that's possible. I'd rather have that direct conversation early than either silently overpromise and deliver something rushed, or refuse outright and damage the relationship.

commonMistakes: Agreeing to everything without assessing feasibility
Refusing outright with no attempt to negotiate
Not communicating with the client at all before deciding
followUps: How would you handle it if the client wasn't willing to compromise?

question: What does your research process look like before you start a new piece?
lookingFor: A genuine, structured research habit that feeds into the final image, not an afterthought.

bullets: Describe concrete research steps, such as reading, reference gathering, or visiting a place
Show how the research actually shapes decisions in the final piece
Balance research with knowing when to stop and start drawing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: If it's a subject I don't know well I'll spend a day or two just reading and pulling reference, historical costume for a period piece, or photos of a specific location if that matters. I keep a moodboard for every project, not to copy from directly but to build a sense of the world before I draw a single line. I try to give myself a hard cutoff though, because I know I can use research as an excuse to avoid the harder work of actually drawing.

commonMistakes: Claiming to skip research and rely purely on imagination
No connection between research and the final image
Research that never ends, avoiding actually making the work
followUps: Can you give an example of research that changed your final piece?

question: Is there a historical illustrator or movement you think shaped illustration as it exists today?
lookingFor: Some grounding in the history of the field beyond contemporary Instagram artists.

bullets: Name a specific historical figure or movement with accurate context
Explain a concrete way their work connects to illustration practice today
Show this is genuine interest, not a memorized fact
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think about the Golden Age American illustrators a lot, especially N.C. Wyeth, because the way he composed action and used strong value contrast for magazine reproduction still shapes how a lot of narrative illustration is built today, even now that we're not limited by print technology in the same way. It's easy to think illustration history starts with whoever's popular online right now, but so much of what reads as 'good composition' to us was worked out under those old commercial constraints. I find that history genuinely useful, not just trivia.

commonMistakes: Naming only contemporary social-media artists with no historical grounding
Vague reference with no accurate detail
No connection drawn to current practice
followUps: How do you think reproduction technology has shaped illustration style over time?

question: What do you think makes panel-to-panel storytelling in comics work well?
lookingFor: Understanding of pacing, panel transitions, and the reader's role in filling gaps between panels.

bullets: Mention the idea of the gutter or the space between panels requiring reader inference
Discuss pacing through panel size and page layout
Give an example from a comic or graphic novel
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A lot of the storytelling actually happens in the gutter, the gap between panels, where the reader has to mentally connect two moments and fill in what happened between them. Panel size and page layout control pacing too, a full-page splash slows the reader right down for something important, while a row of small, similar panels speeds things up. I noticed this clearly reading Nimona, where Stevenson uses really tight, repetitive panels for comedic timing and then breaks the grid completely for emotional beats.

commonMistakes: No mention of the gutter or reader inference
Treating panels as isolated images with no relationship to pacing
No concrete example from an actual comic
followUps: Have you made any sequential work yourself?

question: Tell us about a time a piece of work you were proud of didn't get the response you expected.
lookingFor: Honest reflection on disappointment with evidence of learning or continued motivation, not bitterness.

bullets: Describe a genuine instance of disappointment, such as a competition or portfolio rejection
Show honest processing of the disappointment rather than dismissing it
End with what it taught you or how it changed your approach
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I entered a national student illustration award with a piece I'd spent a month on and didn't even get shortlisted, while a piece I'd made in an afternoon for fun did well elsewhere, which was a strange thing to sit with. It stung for a few days, but going back to the entry criteria I realized the brief wanted something more conceptually daring and I'd played it safe technically instead. Since then I try to ask what a brief is actually rewarding before I decide how much time to sink into polish versus taking a real risk.

commonMistakes: Claiming rejection never bothered them, sounding dismissive
Blaming the judges or process entirely with no self-reflection
No specific lesson or change described
followUps: Has that changed how you approach entering competitions since?

question: What kind of illustration work do you imagine yourself doing after you graduate?
lookingFor: A realistic, informed sense of direction within illustration, showing awareness of the field's variety.

bullets: Name a specific area of illustration, such as editorial, publishing, or games, with reasoning
Show awareness that the field is broad and that direction may shift
Connect it back to what the course offers
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm most drawn to publishing, specifically book covers and interior illustration for young adult fiction, because I like working from someone else's text and finding the image that captures its tone without giving too much away. I know that could shift once I've tried more genres properly, editorial in particular has been growing on me. What matters most to me is staying somewhere I get to keep telling stories visually, whatever specific form that ends up taking, and this course's range of live briefs should help me actually test that out.

commonMistakes: An unrealistically narrow, over-precise plan with no flexibility
No specific area named at all, just 'something in illustration'
No connection to the course
followUps: What's pulling you toward that area specifically?

question: If you had to illustrate the word 'patience' without using a clock or an hourglass, what would you draw?
lookingFor: Genuine, articulate creative thinking under pressure, valuing the reasoning over the final idea.

bullets: Generate an idea live rather than freezing or giving a generic answer
Explain the reasoning behind the image, not just describe it
Show comfort thinking out loud and revising the idea as they talk
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first thought is a seed just barely cracking open underground, nothing showing above the soil yet, because patience is really about the invisible part before any result appears. I might pull back even further and just show the soil with no seed visible at all, and let the title carry the rest, since that forces the viewer to sit with not knowing too. I'd probably sketch both and see which one actually earns the read without over-explaining itself.

commonMistakes: Freezing or refusing to attempt an idea
Giving only a description with no reasoning behind the choice
Reaching for the most obvious cliche with no self-awareness about it
followUps: What would you change about that idea if you had a full day to develop it?
